newsitem.title: USA: Helfer resignation surprises, disappoints US banks.
newsitem.headline: Helfer resignation surprises, disappoints US banks.

text.p: The resignation of top federal bank regulator Ricki Helfer on Friday surprised the banking industry, which praised her as an effective leader.
"It's a surprise and a disappointment," Jim McLaughlin, director of regulatory affairs for the American Bankers Association said.
Helfer, who has chaired the Federal Deposit Insurance Corp since October, 1994, announced Friday she had sent a letter to President Bill Clinton resigning her position from June 1.
"She's done a tremendous job of refocusing FDIC to meet the needs of the banking industry and banking customers as the industry has grown healthy and needs to be more competitive," McLaughlin said.

As the banking industry's health improved, Helfer oversaw staff cuts of one-third at the FDIC. When she took office, the agency was still overwhelmed by failing institutions, but a stronger economy and lower interest rates helped stem the tide and banks reported record profits in 1996.
She also worked with congress to pass legislation last year to recapitalize the Savings Association Insurance Fund.

"The passage of this legislation significantly strengthened the FDIC and it is her important contribution to the financial history of our nation," Kenneth Guenther, executive vice president of the Independent Bankers Association of America, said.

Paul Schosberg, president of the savings industry's trade group, America's Community Bankers, was equally complimentary. Helfer had the group's "deepest appreciation" for her work at the FDIC, he said.
